questions.prompt: What is the core idea of the hedonic treadmill?
choices: Positive gains often lose emotional intensity as they become normal
Every gain is secretly harmful
Only money creates lasting happiness

explanation.gentle: Yes. The gain may stay, but the feeling usually cools.
explanation.direct: Correct. Adaptation lowers emotional intensity after positive change becomes familiar.
explanation.competitive: Right. The win stays, but the buzz gets demoted.

questions.prompt: Which example best fits this chapter?
choices: A promotion feels huge at first and ordinary later
A broken printer stops working
A person forgets a deadline once

explanation.gentle: Yes. A positive gain becomes the new normal.
explanation.direct: Correct. The chapter focuses on adaptation after a positive improvement.
explanation.competitive: That is the pattern. Big win first, regular background later.

questions.prompt: What mistake often follows a gain?
choices: Assuming the first wave of excitement will last unchanged
Believing all improvements are useless
Thinking no one should want success

explanation.gentle: Yes. The emotional forecast is usually too optimistic.
explanation.direct: Correct. People often overestimate how long the feeling of improvement will stay vivid.
explanation.competitive: Exactly. The launch-day high gets treated like a subscription plan.

questions.prompt: Why can a useful gain still feel less powerful later?
choices: Because adaptation lowers salience once the gain is familiar
Because usefulness always vanishes quickly
Because success only matters to other people

explanation.gentle: Yes. Familiar things stop feeling as vivid.
explanation.direct: Correct. Normalization reduces emotional intensity even when practical value remains.
explanation.competitive: Right. The spotlight moves on even if the upgrade still works.

questions.prompt: What is the right boundary for this chapter?
choices: Gains can matter even if novelty fades
All ambition is irrational
Emotional excitement is the only kind of value

explanation.gentle: Yes. The chapter is about fading excitement, not useless gains.
explanation.direct: Correct. Durable utility can remain real even when the emotional premium expires.
explanation.competitive: Exactly. The point is not to trash upgrades, only to stop lying about their hype curve.

questions.prompt: A student wants a new setup because they think it will keep motivation permanently high. What is the better judgment move?
choices: Ask what the setup still improves after the novelty fades
Expect the excitement to stay if the setup is expensive enough
Reject all improvements completely

explanation.gentle: Yes. Check the lasting help, not just the early excitement.
explanation.direct: Correct. The chapter recommends evaluating post-novelty value rather than launch-week emotion.
explanation.competitive: Right. Price the desk for week three, not selfie day.

questions.prompt: What deeper risk appears when adaptation is ignored?
choices: People keep chasing fresh upgrades to replace fading excitement
People become unable to recognize any benefit at all
People stop adapting to positive change

explanation.gentle: Yes. The next gain gets asked to restart the same feeling.
explanation.direct: Correct. Unrecognized adaptation can fuel serial pursuit of new emotional spikes.
explanation.competitive: Exactly. The treadmill speeds up when every cooled-off win is treated like an emergency.

questions.prompt: Which question best captures the hard test in this chapter?
choices: Am I pursuing lasting value or mostly the surge of getting it?
Will other people notice this more than I do?
Can I make this feel exciting forever somehow?

explanation.gentle: Yes. That question separates real benefit from temporary excitement.
explanation.direct: Correct. The chapter's hard diagnostic test distinguishes durable utility from novelty value.
explanation.competitive: That is the knife. It cuts the real upgrade away from the confetti addiction.

questions.prompt: Why is it useful to inspect post-novelty costs as well as benefits?
choices: Because upkeep, pressure, or expense often become clearer after the excitement fades
Because every gain becomes a burden eventually
Because novelty should be ignored completely

explanation.gentle: Yes. The ordinary version of the gain can reveal new responsibilities.
explanation.direct: Correct. Accurate evaluation includes what remains helpful and what becomes costly once routine returns.
explanation.competitive: Right. Some upgrades come with a bill that only shows up after the party.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion best fits this chapter?
choices: Pursue gains that still help after they become ordinary
Only chase what feels thrilling all the time
Avoid every ambitious goal

explanation.gentle: Yes. Lasting value matters more than fading sparkle.
explanation.direct: Correct. Better judgment focuses on durable benefit under familiar conditions.
explanation.competitive: Exactly. Chase what still earns its keep on a boring Tuesday.
